header.title: One meme, step by step
header.intro: Follow a request through the browser, Keycloak, the agent loop, the MCP resource server and Claude, one hop at a time. The **Live test run** tour replays what `tests/test_live.py` actually sent on 2026-10-03. The **Web app** tour adds the browser login that the test skips.
header.diagram_alt: Topology of memes-agent: the browser and Claude API sit outside the token zone; memes-web, the agent, Keycloak and the memes-mcp resource server run on your machine. The highlighted path shows the current step.

1: Map resource owner, client, authorization server and resource server onto running code.
2: What's inside an access token, and who checks iss, aud, exp, scope and sub.
3: An MCP server built with Arcade's framework, protected as a resource server.
4: The hand-written loop: model, then tools, then repeat, with every line understood.
5: Small swappable modules with # EXTEND: points for captions, agentU, federation and Arcade Engine.

flows.name: Web app: login → meme
flows.banner: Reconstructed from the code and not re-run today. Login, onboarding and logout were verified by hand on 2026-10-02. The agent half is the same code the live test ran.

steps.title: Ask Keycloak for a token
steps.what: `dev_token()` uses the **password grant** to get tokens for `dummyuser1`. Only the public `memes-dev` client is allowed to use it. It's a dev shortcut for scripts. Real users log in in the browser with PKCE (see the *Web app* tour).
steps.wire:
POST /realms/memes/protocol/openid-connect/token
  grant_type=password   client_id=memes-dev
  username=dummyuser1   scope=openid

← 200 OK
  access_token  id_token  refresh_token
  expires_in=900  token_type=Bearer
steps.note: The test asked only for `scope=openid`, yet the token carries `memes:read`. That's a *default client scope* on memes-dev, and its audience mapper writes `aud=http://127.0.0.1:8001/mcp` into the token. The scope is what aims the token at the MCP server.
steps.roles: Resource owner: dummyuser1 · Client: memes-dev (the test) · Authorization server: Keycloak
checks: password correct; memes-dev allows direct access grants
quiz: The response also included a refresh_token. Does anything use it?
Not yet. The test uses the access token once. The web app keeps the whole token dict in TokenStore, but nothing reads refresh_token; the # EXTEND: comment in auth.py marks where that would go.

steps.title: Look inside the access token
steps.what: An access token is a signed JWT: header, claims, signature. Anyone can *read* it because it's base64, not encryption. Only Keycloak can *sign* one. The [token inspector](#inspector) lists every claim and who checks it.
steps.inv: A user's identity is `sub`, never `preferred_username` or email.
checks: reading isn't trusting; that happens in step 4

steps.title: Open an MCP session: the client tries the 2026 protocol
steps.what: `MCPToolGateway` builds one HTTP client with `Authorization: Bearer …` as a default header, so *every* MCP request carries the token. The `mcp` 2.2 client first tries the newer `2026-07-28` protocol. The middleware validates the token, which passes. The session manager doesn't support that version and returns 400, so the client falls back.
steps.note: This is the **400 Bad Request** in your test log. It's version negotiation, not an auth failure. A rejected token gets a **401** with `WWW-Authenticate` (step 11).
quiz: How do we know the token passed before the 400?
In arcade-mcp-server, ResourceServerMiddleware wraps the whole MCP app. A bad token would stop there with a 401 and never reach the protocol-version check.

steps.title: Verify the signature with Keycloak's public key
steps.what: The middleware finds the key whose `kid` matches the token header and verifies the RS256 signature. Then it requires `iss`, `aud` and `exp` to match. The key set is fetched once and cached for an hour (`cache_ttl=3600`), so validation is local math. Keycloak isn't asked about each request.
steps.wire:
token header   kid NSvMXk3s…  alg RS256
JWKS           NSvMXk3s…  RS256     use=sig   ← match
               IyuVBgJS…  RSA-OAEP  use=enc

iss == http://localhost:8080/realms/memes   ✓
aud ∋  http://127.0.0.1:8001/mcp            ✓
exp    05:51:12Z > now                       ✓
→ sub becomes context.user_id
steps.inv: The MCP server trusts only JWTs it has validated (signature, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`).
quiz: An admin ends dummyuser1's Keycloak session right now. Does this token stop working?
No. Validation is local, so the token keeps working until exp, 15 minutes after it was issued. That's the trade-off of self-contained JWTs. Short lifetimes plus refresh tokens keep the window small.

steps.title: Classic handshake: initialize
steps.what: The client retries with protocol `2025-11-25`. The server answers 200 with an `Mcp-Session-Id`. Then come `notifications/initialized` (202) and a GET that opens a server→client event stream (200). Each of these HTTP requests passes through the middleware, so the token is validated each time.
steps.wire:
→ POST initialize   protocolVersion=2025-11-25    ← 200
   Mcp-Session-Id: dae75ef7…
→ POST notifications/initialized                  ← 202
→ GET  /mcp   (event stream)                       ← 200
checks: re-validates on every HTTP request, with no per-session trust

steps.title: Discover tools: tools/list
steps.what: The server lists one tool. Arcade names it `Memes_MakeMeme` (app name plus tool name) and builds the JSON schema from the Python signature, so the `Annotated` text becomes the `hints` description. `schemas()` reshapes it into Anthropic's `tools` format.
steps.note: Seam: the `# EXTEND:` in `schemas()` is where tools from a second MCP server or the Arcade Engine would be merged in. The loop doesn't change.

steps.title: Claude, turn 1: decide to call the tool
steps.what: `run_agent` sends one user message, the system prompt and the tool schema. Claude answers with a `tool_use` block and `stop_reason=tool_use`. The loop appends the whole assistant content to `messages` so the next turn sees its own request.
steps.wire:
→ user: "Make me a random meme. Words that describe me:
          ['chaotic', 'nerdy', 'sleepy']"

← stop_reason = tool_use
  {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_015ZKi…",
   "name": "Memes_MakeMeme",
   "input": {"hints": ["chaotic", "nerdy", "sleepy"]}}
steps.inv: Tokens never reach the LLM. Claude sees words and a schema: no token, no `sub`, no MCP URL. The words are data for a tool, not instructions.
checks: your API key, not any user's token
quiz: Could Claude call the MCP server itself?

No. It has no token and doesn't know the URL. All it can do is ask, by emitting a tool_use block. The gateway decides what runs and attaches the credential, which keeps the model out of the trust chain.

steps.title: Run the tool: tools/call
steps.what: The loop passes the `tool_use` to `tools.call()`. The middleware validates the token again and turns `sub` into `context.user_id`, then `make_meme` runs. All three words match catalog tags (10 memes in total), but `matched_hint` is `null`: the 50% influence roll missed, so this pick was uniformly random.
steps.inv: Errors are data. Had this call failed, the gateway would return an `is_error` tool_result for Claude to read rather than crash the loop.
checks: memes:read is in the token; no tool checks it yet

steps.title: Claude, turn 2: wrap up
steps.what: The loop returns a `tool_result` whose `tool_use_id` matches the request. Claude replies with one sentence and `stop_reason=end_turn`. Because that isn't `tool_use`, the loop breaks after 2 steps. `max_steps=4` is only a safety cap.
steps.wire:
→ user: [{"type": "tool_result",
           "tool_use_id": "toolu_015ZKi…",
           "content": "{\"id\": \"trade-offer\", …}"}]

← stop_reason = end_turn
  "Here's your random meme, the classic "Trade Offer", and I hope
   it suits your chaotic, nerdy, sleepy self! 😄"
quiz: Why does the loop keep the meme dict itself instead of parsing Claude's sentence?
The UI needs exact data like image_url. ToolResult.data carries the structured result straight from the tool, so the model's wording can't change it.

steps.title: Close the session and assert
steps.what: Leaving `async with` closes the gateway's exit stack, which sends `DELETE /mcp` to end the session. The test then checks that a meme came back with an `https://` image URL. It passes.
steps.wire:
→ DELETE /mcp   Mcp-Session-Id: …              ← 200
assert result.meme is not None                        ✓
assert result.meme["image_url"].startswith("https://") ✓

steps.title: Extra probe: call with no token
steps.time: tracer only, not part of the test
steps.what: Without a token, the middleware stops the request with **401**. Its `WWW-Authenticate` header points to the server's *protected resource metadata* (RFC 9728), which names Keycloak as the authorization server. An MCP client with no prior setup uses this to find out where to get a token.
steps.wire:
→ POST /mcp    (no Authorization header)
← 401  WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata=
       "http://127.0.0.1:8001/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp"

GET that URL ← 200
{"resource": "http://127.0.0.1:8001/mcp",
 "authorization_servers": ["http://localhost:8080/realms/memes"],
 "bearer_methods_supported": ["header"]}
steps.roles: The resource server advertises which authorization server it trusts

steps.title: Click “Log in”
steps.what: authlib reads Keycloak's discovery document. It creates a random `state`, a `nonce` and a **PKCE** `code_verifier`, and keeps them in the signed session. The redirect carries only the *hash* of the verifier, the `code_challenge`.
steps.note: Sign-up is the same flow plus `prompt=create`, which shows Keycloak's registration page instead.
steps.roles: Client (memes-web) starts the authorization code flow

steps.title: Log in at Keycloak
steps.what: The user types their password into **Keycloak's** page, so memes-web never sees it. Keycloak checks it, starts an SSO session, and ties the `code_challenge` to a one-time code.
steps.inv: Credentials live in the IdP. The app stores only a profile keyed by `sub`.
steps.roles: Resource owner authenticates to the authorization server

steps.title: Redirect back with a one-time code
steps.what: Keycloak sends the browser back to the registered `redirect_uri` with a short-lived `code`. The code travels through the browser, so on its own it's worthless. Redeeming it takes the PKCE verifier and the client secret, and the browser has neither.
quiz: Malware reads the code from browser history. What stops it from redeeming it?
The /token endpoint also wants the code_verifier, which only memes-web's signed session holds, and memes-web's client secret. The code alone gets an error.

steps.title: Swap the code for tokens (back channel)
steps.what: memes-web posts the code, the `code_verifier` and its client credentials straight to Keycloak, server to server. Keycloak hashes the verifier, compares it with the stored challenge, and issues an access token, an ID token and a refresh token. authlib validates the ID token: signature, `iss`, `aud=memes-web` and `nonce`.
steps.wire:
POST /realms/memes/protocol/openid-connect/token
  grant_type=authorization_code   code=…   code_verifier=…
  client_id=memes-web   client_secret=…
← 200 {access_token, id_token, refresh_token, expires_in: 900}
steps.note: Two tokens, two audiences. The **ID token** is for the client (`aud=memes-web`) and says *who logged in*. The **access token** is for the resource server (`aud=…:8001/mcp`) and says *what the bearer may do*. memes-web reads the first and passes the second along unread.
checks: ID token sig · iss · aud · nonce

steps.title: Tokens stay on the server; the browser gets a cookie
steps.what: `TokenStore.put(sub, token)` keeps the tokens in server memory. The browser gets a signed session cookie holding `{sub, name, email}` (SameSite=Lax) and a redirect to `/onboarding` or `/meme`.
quiz: Restart memes-web. What happens on the next click?
TokenStore lives in memory, so it's empty. POST /meme returns 401 {redirect: /login}. Keycloak's SSO session is still alive, so the login finishes without asking for a password.

steps.title: Onboarding: three words, keyed by sub
steps.what: The form posts three words. memes-web checks that each is one lowercase word and saves a `Profile` keyed by `sub`. Name and email come from the ID token, because the IdP owns them.
steps.wire:
INSERT INTO profiles (sub, name, email, words)
  VALUES ("95689752-…", <from ID token>, <from ID token>,
          ["chaotic", "nerdy", "sleepy"])
steps.inv: A user's identity is the Keycloak `sub`: the profile key here, and `context.user_id` in the MCP server.

steps.title: Click “make meme”
steps.what: The browser sends only its cookie. memes-web loads the profile by `sub` and calls `TokenStore.access_token(sub)`, which returns nothing within 30 s of expiry. Then it opens `MCPToolGateway(url, token)` and calls `run_agent(words, tools, llm)`. The token goes to the gateway and the words go to the loop.
steps.note: From here on, the agent path is exactly what the live test ran. Switch to the *Live test run* tour to see real payloads.
checks: exp more than 30 s away, else 401 {redirect: /login}

steps.title: MCP session and token validation
steps.what: Same as live steps 3–6: the version fallback, `initialize` and `tools/list`, each validated against the cached JWKS. The token's `azp` is now `memes-web` instead of `memes-dev`. The server doesn't care which client asked, only whether the token is valid and aimed at it.

steps.title: Claude decides
steps.what: Same as live step 7: words and the schema go in, a `tool_use` comes out. No token crosses this edge.

steps.title: tools/call as this user
steps.what: This token belongs to whoever logged in, so `context.user_id` is *their* `sub`. A per-user feature such as "don't repeat my last memes" would key its state on it (see the EXTEND note in `pick_meme`).

steps.title: Claude wraps up
steps.what: Same as live step 9: the matching `tool_result` goes in, one sentence and `end_turn` come out, and the loop ends.

steps.title: Meme back to the browser
steps.what: memes-web returns `{meme, text}` as JSON, and the page loads the image straight from imgflip. If the agent fails, the user gets a 502 with a plain message and the details go to the server log.

steps.title: Log out
steps.what: memes-web removes the user's tokens from TokenStore, clears the cookie, and redirects to Keycloak's `end_session_endpoint` with `id_token_hint`, so the SSO session ends too (RP-initiated logout).

inspector.title: Token inspector
inspector.intro: The access token from the live run, decoded. Reading a JWT needs no key. Trusting one takes the signature check in live step 4. The right-hand columns show who checks each claim today.

claims.why: Picks which JWKS public key verifies the RS256 signature. Without a valid signature, every other claim could be forged.
Who minted it. Must equal ISSUER, so a token from another realm or IdP is rejected.
Who it's for. Must equal the server's CANONICAL_URL. The memes:read scope's audience mapper puts it there. It stops a token meant for another API from being replayed here.

claims.checked_by: memes-mcp middleware; memes-web TokenStore (30 s leeway)
claims.why: Limits the damage from a leaked token, and it's the only revocation a local validator sees.

claims.checked_by: memes-mcp → context.user_id; memes-web → profile and TokenStore key
claims.why: The stable identity. Emails and usernames can change; sub doesn't.
Says what the bearer may do. The # EXTEND: comment in make_meme marks where a per-tool scope check would go.
Which client asked for the token: memes-dev in the test, memes-web in the browser flow.
Handy for people, never used as identity.

narrative.logs_note: The traced replay is a second run with a scratch script that wraps the project's own classes from the outside, so its session id differs from the pytest run. No repo files were changed.
